questions.question: What is the chemical formula of water?
questions.explanation: Each water molecule has two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom joined together.

questions.question: At what temperature does pure water freeze, in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: Pure water turns into solid ice at 0 °C. Ice takes up more space than the water it came from, so it floats.

questions.question: At what temperature does water boil at sea level, in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: At 100 °C, water turns into a gas. High on mountains, where the air pressure is lower, water boils at a lower temperature.

questions.question: What do we call water when it is a gas?
questions.explanation: Water vapour is invisible. The white cloud you see over a kettle is tiny drops of water, not vapour.

questions.question: Which chemical symbol stands for gold?
questions.explanation: Au comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold. Gold is a soft, yellow metal that does not rust.

questions.question: What is the chemical name of table salt?
questions.explanation: Table salt is made of sodium and chlorine joined together. Both of them are dangerous alone, but safe together.

questions.question: Which element is the lightest of all?
questions.explanation: A hydrogen atom is the simplest atom there is. It has just one proton and one electron.

questions.question: Which gas is often used to fill party balloons so they float up?
questions.explanation: Helium is lighter than air, so a helium balloon rises. Unlike hydrogen, helium does not burn, so it is safe to use.

questions.question: Which metal gets covered in orange-brown rust when it stays wet?
questions.explanation: Rust forms when iron meets water and air. Painting iron keeps the water away and slows rust.

questions.question: Which metal is a liquid at normal room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury is silvery and heavy. It is poisonous, so it is no longer used in most thermometers.

questions.question: Which reddish-brown metal is often used in electric wires?
questions.explanation: Copper lets electricity flow very easily. It is also used for water pipes and some coins.

questions.question: Which element are diamonds made of?
questions.explanation: A diamond is pure carbon with its atoms packed very tightly. It is the hardest natural material.

questions.question: What are the tiny building blocks that all matter is made of?
questions.explanation: Atoms are far too small to see with an ordinary microscope. Everything around you is made of them.

questions.question: Lemons taste sour because they contain which acid?
questions.explanation: Citric acid is also found in oranges and limes. It is a weak acid that is safe to eat.

questions.question: Which gas is made when you mix baking soda and vinegar?
questions.explanation: The bubbles are carbon dioxide. This is why the mixture fizzes up in school volcano experiments.

questions.question: What do we call it when sugar mixes completely into water and seems to disappear?
questions.explanation: The sugar is still there in tiny pieces. The water just tastes sweet.

questions.question: How can you get the salt back from salty water?
questions.explanation: When the water dries into the air, the salt stays behind. People have made sea salt like this for thousands of years.

questions.question: Which metal has the chemical symbol Ag?
questions.explanation: Ag comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver. Argentina is named after it.

questions.question: Fire needs fuel, heat and which gas from the air?
questions.explanation: Without oxygen a fire goes out. That is why a lid on a candle jar puts the flame out.

questions.question: Which gas glows orange-red in glass tubes in bright signs?
questions.explanation: Neon is a rare gas in the air. Electricity makes it glow when it flows through the tube.

questions.question: What do we call a mixture of two or more metals?
questions.explanation: Bronze, made of copper and tin, is an alloy. Alloys are often harder than the pure metals they are made from.

questions.question: Glass is mostly made by melting which natural material?
questions.explanation: Sand is heated to a very high temperature until it melts. Then it cools into clear glass.

questions.question: Most plastic is made from which of these?
questions.explanation: Factories turn oil into plastic. Oil formed deep underground from tiny sea creatures that lived millions of years ago.

questions.question: What do we call it when a solid turns into a liquid?
questions.explanation: Heat makes the tiny particles in a solid move more, so they slide past each other. A melting ice cube is a good example.

questions.question: What is the name of the chart that shows all the chemical elements?
questions.explanation: It puts the elements in order, starting with hydrogen. There are more than 100 elements in the table.

questions.question: Which famous scientist discovered the elements radium and polonium?
questions.explanation: Marie Curie found them with her husband, Pierre. She was born in Poland and named polonium after her home country.

questions.question: In which state of matter is the air around us?
questions.explanation: Air is a mix of different gases. You cannot see it, but you can feel it when the wind blows.

questions.question: Which element is often added to swimming pools to kill germs?
questions.explanation: Chlorine kills germs that could make swimmers ill. Many countries also add a little to tap water to make it safe to drink.

questions.question: What is the 'lead' in a pencil really made of?
questions.explanation: Graphite is a soft, grey form of carbon. It leaves a mark because thin layers rub off on the paper.

questions.question: Which of these changes makes a new substance?
questions.explanation: When wood burns it turns into ash and gases. That is a chemical change, and you cannot turn it back.

questions.question: What do we call two or more atoms joined together?
questions.explanation: A water molecule has three atoms. Some molecules, such as DNA, are made of huge numbers of atoms.

questions.question: Kitchen foil is made from which light, silvery metal?
questions.explanation: Aluminium is very light and does not rust. It can be rolled into sheets thinner than paper.

questions.question: What should you wear in a school laboratory to protect your eyes?
questions.explanation: Safety goggles keep drops and splashes out of your eyes. Chemists wear them when they mix or heat chemicals.

questions.question: Which of these is a mixture?
questions.explanation: Seawater is water with salts and other things mixed in. Pure substances like gold have only one kind of matter.

questions.question: In which of these does sugar dissolve fastest?
questions.explanation: Particles move faster in warm water, so they pull the sugar apart quicker. Sugar does not dissolve in oil.

questions.question: What happens when you pour cooking oil onto water?
questions.explanation: Oil is lighter than water and does not mix with it. That is why oil patches float on puddles.

questions.question: What do we call a substance made of only one kind of atom?
questions.explanation: Gold, oxygen and iron are all elements. Water is not an element because it has two kinds of atoms.

questions.question: What do we call it when a gas cools and turns into drops of liquid?
questions.explanation: Drops on a cold glass of water are condensation. They come from water vapour in the air.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for helium?
questions.explanation: Helium has two letters because H is already taken by hydrogen. Many symbols have a capital letter and a small one.

questions.question: Which state of matter keeps its own shape?
questions.explanation: The particles in a solid are packed tightly and cannot slide past each other. A liquid takes the shape of its container.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?
questions.explanation: Na comes from natrium, a Latin name for sodium. It comes from natron, a salt the ancient Egyptians used to make mummies.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
questions.explanation: K comes from kalium, an old name for potassium. Bananas are a well-known source.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
questions.explanation: Pb comes from plumbum, the Latin word for lead. The word plumber comes from it, because old pipes were made of lead.

questions.question: Which gas makes up most of the air we breathe?
questions.explanation: Air is about 78 per cent nitrogen and 21 per cent oxygen. We breathe nitrogen in and out without using it.

questions.question: What is the pH of pure water?
questions.explanation: pH 7 is neutral. Acids have a pH below 7, and bases (alkalis) have a pH above 7.

questions.question: What colour does blue litmus paper turn when it touches an acid?
questions.explanation: Litmus is a dye made from lichens. It turns red in acid and stays blue in a base.

questions.question: Which Russian chemist made the first widely used periodic table, in 1869?
questions.explanation: Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and by how they behave. His table is the ancestor of the modern one.

questions.question: Helium, neon and argon belong to which group of elements?
questions.explanation: Noble gases hardly ever react with other elements. That is why they are called noble, like aristocrats who keep to themselves.

questions.question: Which particle in an atom has a negative charge?
questions.explanation: Electrons are much lighter than protons and neutrons. They move around the nucleus.

questions.question: Which two kinds of particles are found in the nucleus of an atom?
questions.explanation: The nucleus is tiny but holds almost all the mass of the atom. Electrons are outside it.

questions.question: Brass is made mostly of copper and which other metal?
questions.explanation: Brass is shiny and gold-coloured. It is used for instruments such as trumpets and for door handles.

questions.question: Steel is iron mixed with a small amount of which element?
questions.explanation: Even a little carbon makes iron much harder and stronger. Steel is used in bridges, cars and tools.

questions.question: Why do road crews spread salt on icy roads in winter?
questions.correct: It lowers the freezing point of water
wrong: It raises the freezing point of water
It makes the road surface warmer
questions.explanation: Salty water needs to be colder than 0 °C to freeze. So the ice melts, unless it is very cold.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of carbon dioxide?
questions.explanation: Each molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms. CO, with one oxygen atom, is carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas.

questions.question: Which gas, with the formula CH4, is the main part of natural gas?
questions.explanation: Methane is made of one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms. It has no smell, so a smelly chemical is added for safety.

questions.question: How many oxygen atoms does one molecule of ozone have?
questions.explanation: The oxygen we breathe has two atoms, O2. Ozone has three, O3, and high in the sky it blocks harmful ultraviolet light from the Sun.

questions.question: Dry ice turns straight from a solid into a gas. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide at about minus 78 °C. It never becomes a liquid under normal air pressure.

questions.question: What did alchemists famously try to make from cheaper metals?
questions.explanation: Alchemists never managed it. Their experiments did lead to new tools and methods that early chemists used.

questions.question: Which French chemist, often called the father of modern chemistry, gave oxygen its name?
questions.explanation: Lavoisier showed that burning is a reaction with oxygen. He also helped to start the metric system.

questions.question: Which Swedish chemist invented dynamite and left money for the Nobel Prizes?
questions.explanation: Alfred Nobel wrote in his will that prizes should be given for science, literature and peace.

questions.question: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in physics and in which other subject?
questions.explanation: She was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize, and the first person to win two.

questions.question: What makes fireworks glow in different colours?
questions.explanation: Strontium compounds give red, copper gives blue and barium gives green when they burn.

questions.question: Why do old copper roofs turn green?
questions.correct: Copper reacts with air and water
questions.explanation: The green layer protects the copper underneath. Many old church roofs in Denmark are green for this reason.

questions.question: Chlorine, fluorine and iodine belong to which group of elements?
questions.explanation: The name halogen means salt-former. They react with metals to make salts.

questions.question: Sodium and potassium are soft metals that react fiercely with water. What group are they in?
questions.explanation: They must be stored under oil. They are so soft that you can cut them with a knife.

questions.question: Which of these has the lowest pH, so is the most acidic?
questions.explanation: Lemon juice is about pH 2. Milk is almost neutral, and baking soda is a mild base.

questions.question: Which method separates the different colours in a drop of ink?
questions.explanation: The ink is carried up a strip of paper by water. Different colours travel at different speeds, so they spread out.

questions.question: Which process makes drinking water from seawater by boiling it and cooling the steam?
questions.explanation: The salt stays behind in the pot when the water boils. Ships have used this method for a long time.

questions.question: What do we call a reaction in which a substance burns in oxygen?
questions.explanation: Combustion gives out heat and light. Burning petrol in an engine is combustion too.

questions.question: What do we call a substance that speeds up a reaction but is not used up?
questions.explanation: Cars have catalytic converters that turn harmful gases into less harmful ones.

questions.question: Why does soap help to wash grease off your hands?
questions.correct: It holds on to both water and grease
wrong: It turns grease into a gas
questions.explanation: Soap molecules wrap around grease and let the water carry it away.

questions.question: What do we call large molecules made of long repeating chains, such as plastics?
questions.explanation: Poly means many. Natural polymers include cotton, wool and rubber.

questions.question: What does 24-carat gold mean?
questions.explanation: Pure gold is very soft, so jewellery is often 18-carat or less. It is mixed with other metals to make it harder.

questions.question: Which English scientist said in the early 1800s that each element is made of its own kind of atom?
questions.explanation: Dalton also suffered from colour blindness. For many years it was called Daltonism.

questions.question: What do we call a substance made of two or more elements chemically joined together?
questions.explanation: Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen. Its properties are very different from those of the gases it is made of.

questions.question: What do the elements in the same column of the periodic table have in common?
questions.explanation: Columns are called groups. Copper, silver and gold share a group, and all three have long been used for coins.

questions.question: What is the common name of sodium bicarbonate?
questions.explanation: It is a mild base that helps cakes rise. It is also used for cleaning.

questions.question: Limestone and marble are mainly made of which compound?
questions.explanation: Chalk, seashells and eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate too. Acid makes it fizz.

questions.question: Which two gases are made when electricity splits water?
questions.explanation: Water is H2O, so you get twice as much hydrogen as oxygen. This process is called electrolysis.

questions.question: In which state of matter are the particles furthest apart?
wrong: They are the same in all states
questions.explanation: Gas particles spread out to fill their container. That is why a gas can be squeezed into a smaller space.

questions.question: Which gas is the third most common in dry air, after nitrogen and oxygen?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up almost one per cent of the air. Its name means lazy in Greek, because it does not react.

questions.question: Which element is named after the city of Copenhagen?
questions.explanation: Hafnium comes from Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen. It was discovered there in 1923.

questions.question: In 1825, which light metal was first isolated by the Danish scientist H. C. Ørsted?
questions.explanation: Ørsted is best known for discovering electromagnetism. Aluminium was once more precious than gold.

questions.question: Which scale did Danish chemist Søren Sørensen introduce at the Carlsberg Laboratory in 1909?
questions.explanation: The pH scale measures how acidic or basic a liquid is. It is used for soil, swimming pools and food.

questions.question: What did Swedish chemist Jöns Jacob Berzelius introduce in the early 1800s?
questions.explanation: Thanks to him we write O, Fe and Na. Before that, chemists used drawings and circles.

questions.question: Aluminium is made from which ore?
questions.explanation: Bauxite is often a red-brown rock. Hematite is an ore of iron, galena of lead and cinnabar of mercury.

questions.question: Which mixture of acids can dissolve gold?
questions.explanation: Aqua regia is Latin for royal water. It is a mix of nitric and hydrochloric acids.

questions.question: Iron is galvanised by coating it with which metal?
questions.explanation: Zinc corrodes before iron does, so it protects the iron even where the coating is scratched. Many fences and car parts are galvanised.

questions.question: Which gas smells like rotten eggs?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen sulfide is found around volcanoes and in swamps. It is poisonous in large amounts.

questions.question: The element helium was first detected in what?
questions.explanation: Scientists saw an unknown line in sunlight in 1868. They named it after Helios, the Greek sun god.

questions.question: The name of the gas chlorine comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.explanation: Chlorine gas is yellow-green. The same Greek word gave us chlorophyll, the green colour in leaves.

questions.question: What do we call different forms of the same element, such as diamond and graphite?
questions.explanation: Both are pure carbon, but their atoms are joined in different patterns. This gives very different properties.

questions.question: What do we call atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons?
questions.explanation: Carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. They react in almost the same way, but carbon-14 is radioactive.

questions.question: What do we call an atom that has gained or lost electrons?
questions.explanation: Ions have an electric charge. An atom that loses electrons becomes positive, and one that gains electrons becomes negative.

questions.question: Besides mercury, which element is liquid at normal room temperature?
questions.explanation: Bromine is a dark red-brown liquid with a sharp smell. Its name comes from the Greek word for stench.

questions.question: Which is the most reactive of all the non-metal elements?
questions.explanation: Fluorine reacts with almost every other element, even the noble gas xenon.

questions.question: Why are noble gases like neon and argon so unreactive?
questions.correct: Their outer electron shells are full
questions.explanation: Atoms react to fill their outer shells. Noble gas atoms are already full, so they have no need to.

questions.question: Chemists count atoms in big groups. What is the name of a group of about 6 × 10²³ particles?
questions.explanation: The number is called Avogadro's number. One mole of carbon atoms weighs about 12 grams.

questions.question: What weak attraction between water molecules explains water's high boiling point?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds take extra energy to break, so water boils at a much higher temperature than other small molecules of its size.

questions.question: Which metal has the highest melting point, and was used in old light bulb filaments?
questions.explanation: Tungsten melts at over 3,400 °C. Its symbol is W, from its other name, wolfram.

questions.question: Which metal melts at about 30 °C, so it can melt in your hand?
questions.explanation: Gallium is silvery and soft. A spoon made of it would melt in a cup of hot tea.

questions.question: The name of the gas neon comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.explanation: Neon was discovered in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers. It was the new gas.

questions.question: Why did Mendeleev leave gaps in his periodic table of 1869?
wrong: He thought some elements were not real
He ran out of known gases
He wanted a neat square shape
questions.explanation: He even predicted what the missing elements would be like. Gallium and germanium later matched his guesses.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula of ammonia?
questions.explanation: Ammonia has one nitrogen and three hydrogen atoms. It has a sharp smell and is used in fertilisers and cleaners.

questions.question: An amalgam is an alloy that always contains which metal?
questions.explanation: Dentists used amalgam for fillings. Gold miners also used mercury to collect fine gold.

questions.question: What forms when an acid reacts with a base?
questions.explanation: This is called neutralisation. Hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide make table salt and water.

questions.question: The name of the element phosphorus comes from a Greek word meaning what?
questions.explanation: White phosphorus glows in the dark when it meets air. It was found by an alchemist in 1669.

questions.question: Which English scientist is credited with discovering hydrogen in 1766?
questions.explanation: Cavendish called it inflammable air. Later Lavoisier named it hydrogen, which means water-maker.

questions.question: Which English chemist isolated sodium and potassium using electricity in 1807?
questions.explanation: Davy also invented a safety lamp for miners. Michael Faraday began his career as Davy's assistant.

questions.question: Which is the lightest of all metals?
questions.explanation: Lithium is so light that it floats on oil. It is used in rechargeable batteries.

questions.question: Salt water conducts electricity because it contains what?
questions.explanation: Dissolved salt splits into ions that can carry current. Pure water conducts very poorly.

questions.question: What is the name of the process of getting metal from its ore by heating it?
questions.explanation: In a blast furnace, carbon from coke takes the oxygen away from iron ore and leaves the iron behind.

questions.question: Which metal sits at the centre of the green molecule chlorophyll?
questions.explanation: Plants use chlorophyll to catch sunlight. The haemoglobin in our blood has a similar ring of atoms, but with iron at its centre.

questions.question: What do we call compounds made only of carbon and hydrogen?
questions.explanation: Methane, petrol and paraffin wax are made of hydrocarbons. Carbohydrates, such as sugar, also contain oxygen.

questions.question: What is the chemical name of laughing gas?
questions.explanation: Dentists have used nitrous oxide to ease pain since the 1840s. It is also used to whip cream in spray cans.

questions.question: What colour does sodium make a flame burn in a flame test?
questions.explanation: Many metals give a flame their own colour. The orange-yellow glow of old street lamps also comes from sodium.

questions.question: How many electrons can the first shell of an atom hold?
questions.explanation: The first shell is the one closest to the nucleus. The second shell can hold up to eight electrons.

questions.question: Which element is the second most common in Earth's crust, after oxygen?
questions.explanation: Most rocks and sand contain silicon joined to oxygen. Aluminium comes third.

questions.question: What do we call a reaction that gives out heat?
questions.explanation: Burning is exothermic. Endothermic reactions take heat in, so they can make things feel cold.

questions.question: Which gas bubbles off when zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Hydrogen burns with a small pop. Metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series push it out of acids.
